title: Cocido Madrileño
subtitle: Madrid chickpea stew served in three courses
excerpt: Cocido madrileño is the great dish of Madrid: a pot of chickpeas, vegetables, and several cuts of meat and pork sausage simmered together for hours in one pot. It is served in three courses -- first the broth with pasta, then the vegetables and chickpeas, then the meats. It is the ultimate Sunday dish and one of the defining meals of Spanish cooking.
sourceNotes: Cocido madrileño is the Sunday dish of Madrid and one of the most important dishes in Spanish cuisine. It descends from the medieval Jewish adafina (Sabbath stew) that simmered overnight. The dish is a direct relative of the French pot-au-feu, the Italian bollito misto, and the Portuguese cozido. The three-course service is the traditional way of eating it: the fat, starchy broth first, then the vegetables, then the meat.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze separately: broth, chickpeas, and meats. Works well for meal prep.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large pot. Improves over several days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Better the next day. The broth clarifies and deepens.

content.text: The chickpeas must be soaked overnight. The soup pasta (fideos or thin vermicelli) is added to the broth at the end. If you cannot find morcilla, use black pudding. The stew should barely simmer -- a rolling boil makes cloudy broth and tough meat.

Drain the soaked {{chickpeas-dried}} chickpeas. Put them in a very large pot with {{beef-shin}} beef shin, {{chicken-thigh}} chicken, {{smoked-bacon}} smoked bacon, {{garlic}} garlic, {{bay-leaves}} bay leaves, and {{black-peppercorns}} peppercorns. Cover with 3 litres of cold water. Bring slowly to a boil, skimming any foam.

Reduce to a low simmer. Add {{chorizo}} chorizo and {{black-pudding}} black pudding. Simmer for 2 hours. After 1.5 hours, add {{carrots}} carrots and {{potatoes-floury}} potatoes. After 2 hours, add {{cabbage-savoy}} cabbage. Season with {{salt-table}} salt. Continue until all the vegetables and meat are tender.

Ladle the broth into a separate pot. Boil {{pasta-dried}} pasta in the broth until tender. Serve the broth and pasta first as a soup. Then serve the chickpeas and vegetables on a separate plate. Then slice the meats and serve as the final course.

items.symptom: The chickpeas are still firm after 2 hours
items.cause: Old dried chickpeas, or not soaked long enough.
items.fix: Keep simmering. Do not add salt until the chickpeas are tender -- salt toughens them. Old chickpeas can take up to 3.5 hours.

content.text: Cocido madrileño is the Sunday lunch of Madrid. The dish appears in literature and painting from the 17th century onwards as the great popular dish of the Spanish capital. Restaurants in Madrid still serve it -- not as a historic curio but as an ongoing living dish. The three-course service is unusual in Spanish cooking and gives the dish a special ceremonial quality.
